claim: CRIg+ TRMs are enriched at the capsular area of pancreatic islets in NOD mice.
source: In the pancreas, CRIg+ TRMs were enriched at the capsular area of the islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), exhibiting a perivascular distribution (Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing immunostaining data.

claim: The abundance of islet CRIg+ macrophages in NOD mice is negatively correlated with the risk of diabetes onset.
source: We have previously found that the abundance of islet CRIg+ macrophages in NOD mice was negatively correlated with the risk of diabetes onset in these animals (Fu et al., 2012), suggesting a disease-suppressing role of CRIg+ TRMs in T1D.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to previous work (Fu et al., 2012).

claim: Intact islets free from autoimmune infiltration are associated with more abundant peri-islet CRIg+ TRMs.
source: We found that intact islets (free from autoimmune infiltration) were associated with more abundant peri-islet CRIg+ TRMs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In insulitic islets, there is a lack of CRIg expression in TRMs, especially in peri-islet areas succumbed to infiltration.
source: In contrast, in insulitic islets, there was a lack of CRIg expression in TRMs, especially in those peri-islet areas succumbed to infiltration (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A.

claim: CRIg+ TRMs function as a local barrier to prevent immune infiltration into pancreatic islets.
source: These results suggest that CRIg+ TRMs may function as a local barrier to prevent immune infiltration into pancreatic islets.
evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observed correlation between CRIg+ TRM abundance and insulitis severity.

claim: Genetic ablation of CRIg significantly exacerbates the severity of insulitis in NOD mice.
source: Indeed, genetic ablation of CRIg significantly exacerbated the severity of insulitis, reflected by a massive infiltration of leukocytes in most islets (Figure 1B), supporting a critical role of CRIg for these CRIg+ TRMs to suppress insulitis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by histological data shown in Figure 1B comparing NOD and NOD/CRIg KO mice.

claim: The fraction of Treg cells is reduced in pancreatic islets of NOD/CRIg KO mice compared to wildtype NOD mice.
source: Comparing to age-matched wildtype NOD mice, CRIg knockout (KO) mice exhibited an altered balance between regulatory and effector T cells, reflected by: (i) The fraction of Treg cells was reduced in pancreatic islets (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C.

claim: The reduction of Treg abundance in CRIg KO mice is not seen in lymphoid organs.
source: Such a reduction of Treg abundance was not seen in lymphoid organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), supporting a tissue-specific immunoregulatory role of CRIg.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ratio between pancreatic Treg and CD8+ T cells is reduced in NOD/CRIg KO mice.
source: (ii) The ratio between pancreatic Treg and CD8+ T cells was also reduced in NOD/CRIg KO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells isolated from pancreatic islets of NOD/CRIg KO mice exhibit significantly increased production of IFN-γ.
source: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells isolated from the pancreatic islets, not lymphoid organs, of NOD/CRIg KO mice exhibited significantly increased production of IFN-γ (Figure 1D), which is a key pathogenic cytokine in T1D development (Feuerer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D and citation to Feuerer et al., 2009.

claim: IFN-γ is a key pathogenic cytokine in T1D development.
source: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells isolated from the pancreatic islets, not lymphoid organs, of NOD/CRIg KO mice exhibited significantly increased production of IFN-γ (Figure 1D), which is a key pathogenic cytokine in T1D development (Feuerer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Feuerer et al., 2009.

claim: CRIg+ TRMs interact with T cells in close proximity in pre-diabetic islets.
source: Immunostaining of pre-diabetic islets (with ongoing insulitis) from NOD mice showed that there were cell clusters containing both CRIg+ TRMs and T cells in close proximity, suggesting a cell-cell contact between CRIg+ TRMs and T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is stated based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Plate-coated CRIg-Ig suppresses T cell proliferation in vitro.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Vogt et al., 2006; Fu et al., 2012), we found that plate-coated CRIg-Ig, not control Ig, suppressed T cell proliferation in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by in vitro proliferation assay data in Figure 2A and citations to previous work.

claim: The presence of CRIg-Ig during the first 24 hours is sufficient to suppress T cell proliferation.
source: We found that the presence of CRIg-Ig during the first 24 hr was sufficient to suppress T cell proliferation, to an extent similar to the condition where CRIg-Ig was present all time of the culture (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by time-course proliferation assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: When CRIg-Ig is only present during the last 48 hours of culture, its suppressive effect on T cell proliferation is largely abolished.
source: In contrast, when CRIg-Ig was only present during the last 48 hr, its suppressive effect on T cell proliferation was largely abolished (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by time-course proliferation assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: CRIg interferes with early T cell activation.
source: Therefore, CRIg interferes early T cell activation.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the time-course experiments showing CRIg effects are most prominent in the first 24 hours.

claim: CRIg-Ig potently suppresses the upregulation of CD69 and CD25 in T cells.
source: In a time-course assay, the majority of T cells exhibited an upregulation of both CD69 and CD25 within 17 hr. CRIg-Ig potently suppressed the upregulation of both CD69 and CD25 in T cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: The presence of plate-bound CRIg-Ig suppresses the phosphorylation of ZAP70, ERK1/2, AKT and ribosomal protein S6.
source: Using phosphorylation assays, we found that the presence of plate-bound CRIg-Ig suppressed the phosphorylation of ZAP70, ERK1/2, AKT and ribosomal protein S6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: CRIg-Ig dampens several pathways crucial for early T cell activation, including the most proximal signaling complex (ZAP70), the ERK-MAPK pathway (ERK1/2, and S6) and the AKT-MTOR pathway (AKT, S6).
source: These data suggest that CRIg-Ig dampens several pathways that are crucial for early T cell activation, including the most proximal signaling complex (ZAP70), the ERK-MAPK pathway (ERK1/2, and S6) and the AKT-MTOR pathway (AKT, S6).
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the phosphorylation data showing effects on multiple signaling molecules.

claim: Complement components are not involved in CRIg-mediated T cell suppression.
source: Using a specific monoclonal antibody (mAb) (clone 14G8) (ref. [Gorgani et al., 2008]) that can block the binding of CRIg to C3 components, we found that 14G8 did not abolish T cell suppression by CRIg, suggesting that complements were not involved in CRIg-mediated T cell suppression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated based on blocking antibody experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CRIg can attenuate TCR activation in serum-free condition, which is deprived of complements.
source: This notion was further supported by that CRIg can attenuate TCR activation in serum-free condition, which was deprived of complements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in serum-free conditions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CRIg can bind to activated T cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that CRIg can bind to activated T cells, in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by binding assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: CRIg-Ig exhibits stronger binding to T cells at their early stage of in vitro activation (12 hr and 24 hr) compared to late stage (72 hr).
source: Interestingly, we observed stronger binding of CRIg-Ig to T cells at their early, not late, stage of in vitro activation (12 hr and 24 hr versus 72 hr) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by time-course binding assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: CRIg-Ig can bind to activated Treg cells, but with lower binding intensity compared to Tconv cells.
source: CRIg-Ig can also bind to activated Treg cells. However, in any analyzed concentration of CRIg-Ig, or time-point, the binding intensity was lower comparing to that for Tconv cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by binding assay data comparing Treg and Tconv cells in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Treg cells are less sensitive to CRIg-mediated suppression compared to Tconv cells.
source: Consistent with this, Treg cells were less sensitive to CRIg-mediated suppression (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is stated and supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: CRIg preferentially suppresses effector T cells via binding to a putative receptor in these cells at their early stage of activation and attenuating early TCR activation signaling.
source: In summary, CRIg preferentially suppresses effector T cells via binding to a putative receptor in these cells at their early stage of activation and attenuating early TCR activation signaling.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including binding and signaling assays.

claim: CRIg-Ig enhances the generation of iTreg cells at any given dose of TGF-β.
source: As expected, TGF-β promoted iTreg differentiation in a dose-dependent manner. At any given dose of TGF-β, CRIg-Ig further enhanced the generation of iTreg cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by iTreg differentiation assay data in Figure 3A.

claim: CRIg-mediated enhancement of iTreg generation is more profound when TGF-β concentration is relatively low.
source: CRIg-mediated enhancement of iTreg generation was more profound when TGF-β concentration was relatively low (e.g., there was a more than two-fold increase of iTreg induction by CRIg-Ig with 0.2 ng/ml TGF-β) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by dose-response data in Figure 3A.

claim: CRIg-Ig alone does not induce the conversion of Tconv cells into iTreg cells in the absence of TGF-β.
source: In the absence of TGF-β, CRIg-Ig alone did not induce the generation of iTreg cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by iTreg differentiation assay with anti-TGF-β neutralizing antibody shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CRIg-Ig induces a 2-fold increase of Treg generation in antigen-stimulated conditions.
source: Compared with control Ig, CRIg-Ig induced a 2-fold increase of Treg generation (Figure 3C), suggesting a role of CRIg in promoting Ag-stimulated Treg generation.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by antigen-stimulated Treg generation assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: CRIg+ macrophages significantly enhance Ag-induced iTreg generation compared to CRIg- macrophages.
source: Using an in vitro Ag-stimulated iTreg generation condition, we found that even though CRIg- macrophages can modestly promote Ag-induced iTreg generation, this effect was significantly elevated by CRIg+ macrophages (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by co-culture assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: A 2-week in vivo CRIg-Ig treatment preferentially enhances pTreg development in pancreatic islets, not pancreas-draining or non-draining lymph nodes.
source: We found that a 2-week in vivo CRIg-Ig treatment preferentially enhanced pTreg development in pancreatic islets, not pancreas- draining or non-draining lymph nodes (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by adoptive transfer experiment data in Figure 3E.

claim: The generation of Treg cells is compromised in the absence of CRIg in the pancreas, but not in pancreas-draining or non-draining lymph nodes.
source: The generation of Treg cells was compromised in the absence of CRIg (Figure 3F). Of note, this reduction only occurred in the pancreas, not in pancreas-draining or non-draining lymph nodes, suggesting a local microenvironment-specific role of CRIg in regulating pTreg generation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by adoptive transfer experiment comparing NOD and NOD/CRIg KO mice in Figure 3F.

claim: Helios- peripherally-induced Treg (pTreg) cells are preferentially reduced in pancreas and colon of NOD/CRIg KO mice, compared with wildtype controls.
source: Consistent with the role of CRIg in affecting Treg cells at tissue sites, we found that Helios- peripherally-induced Treg (pTreg) (Shevach and Thornton, 2014) cells were preferentially reduced in pancreas and colon of NOD/CRIg KO mice, compared with wildtype controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G and citation to Shevach and Thornton, 2014.

claim: pTreg cells in the lung are not affected by CRIg deficiency.
source: In contrast, since there was no CRIg expression in lung macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), pTreg cells in the lung were not affected by CRIg deficiency.
evidence: The claim is stated based on the absence of CRIg expression in lung and flow cytometry data in Figure 3G.

claim: Plate-bound CRIg-Ig more potently suppresses the phosphorylation of AKT under iTreg induction condition.
source: Under iTreg induction condition, plate-bound CRIg-Ig more potently suppressed the phosphorylation of AKT (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in Figure 3H.

claim: The phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein is more significantly suppressed by CRIg-Ig under iTreg induction condition.
source: Similarly, the phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein, a downstream target of mTOR pathway was also more significantly suppressed by CRIg-Ig (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in Figure 3I.

claim: CRIg-Ig does not enhance TGF-β induced phosphorylation of Smad2/3.
source: However, CRIg-Ig did not enhance TGF-β induced phosphorylation of Smad2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CRIg-Ig potentiates iTreg generation via suppressing AKT-MTOR pathway.
source: Thus, CRIg-Ig potentiates iTreg generation via suppressing AKT-MTOR pathway.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the phosphorylation data showing suppression of AKT and S6 but not Smad2/3.

claim: About 50% of control iTreg cells lose their expression of Foxp3 after 3 days of restimulation.
source: After 3 days, about 50% of control iTreg cells lost their expression of Foxp3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: In the presence of plate-bound CRIg-Ig, a significantly higher fraction of iTreg cells retain Foxp3 after restimulation.
source: In contrast, in the presence of plate-bound CRIg-Ig, a significantly higher fraction of iTreg cells retained Foxp3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: The instability of Foxp3 expression in restimulated iTreg cells is repressed by CRIg-Ig, especially when the cells undergo multiple divisions.
source: The loss of Foxp3 in restimulated iTreg cells was exacerbated over the course of cell dividing. This instability of Foxp3 expression was repressed by CRIg-Ig, especially when the cells underwent multiple divisions (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cell division analysis data in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression level of Foxp3 protein on a per cell basis is higher in restimulated iTreg cells in the presence of CRIg-Ig.
source: Moreover, the expression level of Foxp3 protein on a per cell basis was also higher in restimulated iTreg cells in the presence of CRIg-Ig, compared to that in control group (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by MFI analysis data in Figure 4D.

claim: The Treg-stabilizing effect of CRIg is TGF-β independent.
source: Notably, this Treg-stabilizing effect of CRIg is TGF-β independent, because we have added an anti-TGF-β neutralizing mAb to eliminate any trace amount of TGF-β.
evidence: The claim is stated based on the experimental design using anti-TGF-β neutralizing antibody.

claim: CRIg preconditioned iTreg cells exhibit an enhanced suppressive capacity in an in vitro Treg suppression assay.
source: In line with a Treg–stabilizing effect, CRIg preconditioned iTreg cells exhibited an enhanced suppressive capacity in an in vitro Treg suppression assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Treg suppression assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CpG sites in Foxp3 CNS2 region of control iTreg cells are highly methylated.
source: As expected, CpG sites in Foxp3 CNS2 region of control iTreg cells were highly methylated (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 4E.

claim: A similar profile of CpG methylation is observed in CRIg iTreg cells compared to control iTreg cells.
source: A similar profile of CpG methylation was observed in CRIg iTreg cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 4E.

claim: CRIg-promoted iTreg stability is not a consequence of demethylation in Foxp3 CNS2 region.
source: These data suggest that CRIg-promoted iTreg stability is not a consequence of demethylation in Foxp3 CNS2 region.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the methylation data showing no difference between control and CRIg iTreg cells.

claim: The presence of CRIg-Ig results in a significantly higher fraction of restimulated iTreg cells retaining their expression of Foxp3 in the presence of IL-2.
source: In contrast, the presence of CRIg-Ig resulted in a significantly higher fraction of restimulated iTreg cells retaining their expression of Foxp3, in the presence of IL-2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by dose-response data with IL-2 in Figure 4F.

claim: CRIg induced iTreg cells express a higher level of IL-2Rβ.
source: CRIg induced iTreg cells expressed a higher level of IL-2Rβ (Figure 4G), suggesting an enhanced responsiveness of these cells to IL-2.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4G.

claim: IL-2-induced STAT5 phosphorylation in iTreg cells is significantly enhanced by CRIg-Ig.
source: IL-2-induced STAT5 phosphorylation in iTreg cells was significantly enhanced by CRIg-Ig (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by phosphorylation assay data in Figure 4H.

claim: CRIg retains Foxp3 expression in iTreg cells by enhancing their responsiveness to IL-2.
source: Therefore, CRIg retains Foxp3 expression in iTreg cells by enhancing their responsiveness to IL-2.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the IL-2Rβ expression and STAT5 phosphorylation data.

claim: Control and CRIg iTreg cells exhibit similar degrees of engraftments after adoptive transfer into neonatal NOD mice.
source: Control and CRIg iTreg cells exhibited similar degrees of engraftments (Figure 5B,C), suggesting that preconditioning with CRIg did not affect homeostatic survival and expansion of these adoptively transferred cells.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: iTreg cells generated in the presence of CRIg-Ig show enhanced stability under lymphopenic condition.
source: However, iTreg cells generated in the presence of CRIg-Ig showed an enhanced stability under lymphopenic condition.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by adoptive transfer experiment data in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: A significantly higher fraction of transferred CRIg-iTreg cells maintain their expression of Foxp3 in spleen after adoptive transfer.
source: In spleen, a significantly higher fraction of transferred CRIg-iTreg cells maintained their expression of Foxp3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5B.

claim: Preconditioning with CRIg before adoptive transfer retains a significantly higher percentage of Foxp3 expression in pancreatic islets.
source: However, preconditioning with CRIg before the adoptive transfer retained a significantly higher percentage of Foxp3 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5C.

claim: iTreg cells generated by TGF-β plus CRIg-Ig are more stable in vivo.
source: Thus, iTreg cells generated by TGF-β plus CRIg-Ig are more stable in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the adoptive transfer experiments showing enhanced Foxp3 retention.

claim: Cross-linking CRIg with an anti-CRIg mAb (clone 17C9) significantly enhances TGF-β-induced iTreg generation in vitro.
source: Our in vitro studies revealed that cross-linking CRIg with an anti-CRIg mAb (e.g., clone 17C9) significantly enhanced TGF-β-induced iTreg generation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by in vitro iTreg differentiation assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serum half-life of CRIg-Ig is significantly prolonged when an anti-CRIg mAb (clone 17C9) is administered simultaneously with CRIg-Ig.
source: In vivo analyses revealed that serum half-life of CRIg-Ig was significantly prolonged when an anti-CRIg mAb (clone 17C9) was administrated simultaneously with CRIg-Ig (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by ELISA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Anti-CRIg mAb alone does not alter the compositions of T cells in vivo, including Treg cells.
source: Moreover, anti-CRIg mAb alone did not alter the compositions of T cells in vivo, including Treg cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The ratios between Treg cells and CD4+ Tconv cells in pancreatic islets are significantly increased in CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg complex treated mice.
source: Of note, the ratios between Treg cells and CD4+ Tconv cells in pancreatic islets were significantly increased in CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg complex treated mice, with about 50% of the mice exhibited a robust response (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A.

claim: The ratios between Treg and CD8+ T cells in pancreatic islets are increased in CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg complex treated mice.
source: Similar results were observed in the ratios between Treg and CD8+ T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A.

claim: The effect of in vivo CRIg modulation on Treg/effector T cell ratios is only seen at tissue sites (pancreatic islets), not in lymphoid organs.
source: Of note, such an effect was only seen at tissue sites (pancreatic islets), not in lymphoid organs, such as panLNs (Figure 6B), or spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6B and 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In vivo CRIg modulation increases the proportion of Helios- Treg cells in pancreatic islets.
source: Interestingly, in vivo CRIg modulation increased the proportion of Helios- Treg cells (Figure 6C), indicating an enhanced generation of pTreg cells (Thornton et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6C and citation to Thornton et al., 2010.

claim: A significantly increased proportion of islet Treg cells from CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg treated mice are ICOShi.
source: We found that a significantly increased proportion of islet Treg cells from CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg treated mice were ICOShi (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D.

claim: In vivo CRIg modulation significantly reduces IFN-γ production in CD4+ Tconv cells from pancreatic islets.
source: As a consequence of CRIg on helper T (Th) cell differentiation, we observed a significantly reduced IFN-γ production in CD4+ Tconv cells from pancreatic islets (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6E.

claim: IL-17+ T (Th17) cell differentiation is significantly increased in pancreatic islets of CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg complex treated mice.
source: However unexpectedly, IL-17+ T (Th17) cell differentiation was significantly increased in pancreatic islets of CRIg-Ig/anti-CRIg complex treated mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6F.

claim: CRIg is almost completely absent in the liver from neonatal (day one post birth) mice.
source: However, in contrast, CRIg was almost completely absent in the liver from neonatal (day one post birth) mice, though F4/80+ Kupffer cells were readily detected (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A.

claim: CRIg is absent in macrophages from the pancreas in neonatal mice.
source: We confirmed the absence of CRIg expression in macrophages from other tissues, including the pancreas in neonatal mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7B.

claim: CRIg is not constitutively expressed in macrophages, rather, is contingent upon extrinsic signals arisen postnatally.
source: Therefore, CRIg is not constitutively expressed in macrophages, rather, is contingent upon extrinsic signals arisen postnatally.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the absence of CRIg in neonatal macrophages.

claim: There is a sharp increase of CRIg expression in macrophages around the time of weaning.
source: Clearly, there was a sharp increase of CRIg expression in macrophages around the time of weaning, a time-point when mice were exposed to environmental cues (Laukens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by longitudinal flow cytometry data in Figure 7C and citation to Laukens et al., 2016.

claim: Antibiotic treatment significantly decreases the fractions of CRIg+ TRMs at tissue sites (colon and pancreas).
source: Though the fraction of CRIg+ TRMs in peritoneal cavity was not affected by antibiotic treatment, in contrast, at tissue sites (colon and pancreas), the fractions of CRIg+ TRMs were significantly decreased (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 7D-F.

claim: Antibiotic treatment significantly diminishes CRIg expression on a per cell basis in macrophages at all examined locations.
source: Of note, at all examined locations, antibiotic treatment significantly diminished CRIg expression on a per cell basis in macrophages (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by MFI data in Figures 7D-F.

claim: CRIg expression in TRMs is induced postnatally by microbial signals.
source: These data suggest that CRIg expression in TRMs is induced postnatally by microbial signals.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the antibiotic treatment data showing reduced CRIg expression.

claim: TRMs (both CRIg+ and CRIg- subsets) abundantly express retinoic acid (RA) receptors (RAR).
source: We have found that TRMs (both CRIg+ and CRIg- subsets) abundantly express retinoic acid (RA) receptors (RAR) (Figure 7G), suggesting that these cells are able to respond to RA.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 7G.

claim: ATRA retains the expression of CRIg in cultured CRIg+ macrophages to a level comparable to that in freshly isolated CRIg+ macrophages.
source: In the absence of ATRA, the expression of CRIg decreased (reflected by a lower MFI of CRIg) after 3-day culture. In contrast, ATRA retained the expression of CRIg, to a level comparable to that in freshly isolated CRIg+ macrophages (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by in vitro culture data in Figure 7H.

claim: ATRA increases CRIg expression in isolated CRIg- macrophages.
source: Interestingly, ATRA also increased CRIg expression in isolated CRIg- macrophages (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that RA signaling may be involved in inducing CRIg expression in macrophages.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by in vitro culture data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BMS 493 significantly reduces CRIg expression in peritoneal F4/80hi TRMs.
source: Compared with control vehicle-treated mice, BMS 493 significantly reduced CRIg expression in peritoneal, but not pancreatic F4/80hi TRMs (Figure 7I,J).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 7I and 7J.

claim: BMS 493 treatment reduces the expression of CRIg in peritoneal macrophages in an adoptive transfer setting.
source: Consistently, BMS 493 treatment also reduced the expression of CRIg in peritoneal macrophages in an adoptive transfer setting, where donor CRIg+ macrophages were purified from congenically-labeled mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by adoptive transfer experiment data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RA signaling is involved in regulating CRIg expression in TRMs in a tissue-specific manner.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that RA signaling is involved in regulating CRIg expression in TRMs in a tissue-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the ATRA and BMS 493 experiments showing differential effects in different tissues.

claim: CRIg+ macrophages can be detected in peritoneal cavity and most digestive organs, including pancreas, liver, small and large intestines of both C57BL/6 (B6) and NOD mice.
source: CRIg+ macrophages can be detected in most digestive organs at steady state, including the pancreas, liver, colon and peritoneal cavity of both C57BL/6 (B6) and NOD mice (Figure 1-figure supplement 1A, B and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by immunostaining and flow cytometry data in Figure 1-figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: There is no CRIg+ cell in the lung in both B6 and NOD mouse strains.
source: There was no CRIg+ cell in the lung in both mouse strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by immunostaining and flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The expression of CRIg is not detected in lymphoid-lineage cells, including T cells, B cells and NK cells.
source: The expression of CRIg was not detected in lymphoid-lineage cells, including T cells, B cells and NK cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The expression of CRIg is restricted to TRMs.
source: Thus, the expression of CRIg is restricted to TRMs.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the tissue distribution data showing CRIg expression only in macrophages.

claim: CRIg is exclusively expressed in TRMs.
source: CRIg is exclusively expressed in TRMs (Helmy et al., 2006; Vogt et al., 2006; Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Macrophages from lymphoid organs do not express CRIg.
source: Macrophages from lymphoid organs do not express CRIg.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: CRIg is absent in other immune cells, including T cells, B cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, and neutrophils.
source: CRIg is also absent in other immune cells, including T cells, B cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, and neutrophils (Helmy et al., 2006; Vogt et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to previous work.
